article.Citation/Title: Hollister, L. E., Shelton, J., & Krieger, G. (1969). A controlled comparison of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and dextroamphetamine in alcoholics. American Journal of Psychiatry, 125(10), 1352-1357.
article.SourcePDF: alcohol/Hollister, L. E., Shelton, J., & Krieger, G. (1969). A controlled comparison of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).pdf
article.Outcome: 48 vs 49 (LSD vs dextroamphetamine mean Drinking Behavior Scale change score, 6-month follow-up; NS)
article.InterventionDescription: Single oral dose LSD-25 600mcg or dextroamphetamine 60mg (randomized, blinded), given in a dedicated hospital room; 8-hour supervised session with two psychiatrist visits; VA hospital inpatient setting.

ae_events.Description: Five of 72 patients died within one year of study entry; four from alcohol-related complications (accidents, suicide, decompensated cirrhosis), one of unknown cause.
Moderate agitation occasionally required additional psychiatrist attention and reduced sensory input; two patients needed intramuscular chlorpromazine 50mg for more severe agitation.
Grand mal seizure during a period of agitation in one patient with prior history of alcohol-withdrawal ('rum fits') seizures; no injury resulted.
Vomiting occurred in two other cases; nausea was otherwise reported as infrequent.
Moderate confusion in one patient required extended hospitalization for a further 48 hours beyond the standard 48-hour discharge window.

article.Outcome: Discussion states 'the choice of a six-month follow-up period appeared justified as the least biasing and most feasible evaluation period' -- the authors' own designation of a primary evaluation timepoint (precedence rule 1). Table 3 ('Six-Month Follow-Up Results in 45 Alcoholic Patients') footnotes give the mean DBS change scores directly: 'Mean change score on the DBS=48' (LSD) and 'Mean change score on the DBS=49' (dextroamphetamine), footnoted '(Not significant, analysis of variance.)'. The two-month result (Table 2, F=8.85, 1&50 df, p<.01) is NOT used as Outcome because the authors explicitly frame it as an early/transient effect superseded by the six-month analysis ('after six months the results were alike for both treatment groups' per the abstract). Table 3's categorical breakdown (Abstinent/Social/Same/Worse by arm) was not used instead because the printed dextroamphetamine-column counts (7+2+5+1=15) do not sum to the stated N=19 for that arm -- an internal inconsistency flagged here per the anti-fabrication rule rather than silently corrected or used.
article.SD: Table 3's footnote reports only the qualitative result 'Not significant, analysis of variance' for the six-month comparison, with no F value, t value, or df printed (unlike the two-month comparison, which prints 'F=8.85; 1 and 50 df; p<.01'). Because no statistic value is paired with the six-month Outcome, this is coded '.' rather than substituting the two-month F, which belongs to a different (non-primary) analysis.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: 45. Table 3 title: 'Six-Month Follow-Up Results in 45 Alcoholic Patients', with N=26 (LSD) and N=19 (dextroamphetamine) by arm (26+19=45), consistent with the text: 'Only 45 patients were followed for six months, 27 dropping out' (72-45=27).

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: 13/14 criteria met. Not described: sample_size_power -- no a priori or post hoc statistical power calculation or discussion appears anywhere in the article. All other elements are explicitly described: objective (Discussion states the study's purpose), design and setting (Method: VA Hospital, Palo Alto, blind-controlled single-dose comparison), eligibility (Patients section: age 21-50, VA admission, recent acute alcoholic episode, residency/job stability, disqualifying conditions listed), intervention and comparator (Treatment section: LSD-25 600mcg vs dextroamphetamine 60mg, session structure), outcomes (Evaluations section: Drinking Behavior Scale and its categories), randomization ('assigned in a random fashion'), blinding (patient- and interviewer-blind procedures described, including the explicit caveat that staff would likely become aware of differences), statistical methods (ANOVA, chi-square named), results (detailed tables), harms (dedicated paragraph on agitation, seizure, vomiting, and prolonged hospitalization), and funding/COI (PHS grant and drug-supplier acknowledgment). n_met=13 >= 13, so MethodologyDescribedYN=1.

article.Pos Result Y/N: 0 (null). At the primary (six-month) timepoint the two arms are essentially indistinguishable (mean DBS change 48 vs 49, NS by ANOVA); the early two-month advantage for LSD explicitly 'vanished' by six months per the authors. Judged on the primary comparison (LSD vs active comparator), not on within-arm pre/post improvement, because this is a two-arm comparator trial rather than a single-arm design.
article.Clincial Trial YN: 1, consistent with the eligibility screen: a prospectively planned, randomized, blind-controlled single-dose trial of LSD vs dextroamphetamine with defined enrollment (72 patients), an assigned regimen, and prospective outcome assessment (DBS at 2, 6, and 12 months).
article.RandomizationYN: 1. 'These medications were administered orally in a similar form, being assigned in a random fashion.'
article.BlindingYN: 1. Patients were blinded ('patients were given as little concrete information as possible about the drugs to be tested... the actual drugs were not named nor any mention made of a control'), and the outcome interviewer was blinded ('The interviewer was completely divorced from the treatment program and had no knowledge of the treatment received by any individual patient').
article.Double+Blind: 0, not 1, despite BlindingYN=1. The article explicitly states 'it was expected that patients might ultimately become aware that two treatments were being used and that most certainly staff members would become aware of differences in patients treated' -- the administering/attending staff during the 8-hour dosing session were not blinded, only the patient and the follow-up interviewer were. This falls short of a true double-blind design (patient + treating staff both blinded), so Double+Blind=0 while BlindingYN=1 reflects the patient- and rater-blinding that was achieved. Judgment call, flagged per the field's must-not-contradict rule (satisfied: 0 does not exceed BlindingYN).
article.Comparator: 1. Active comparator design: dextroamphetamine 60mg oral vs LSD-25 600mcg oral, randomly assigned, administered and evaluated identically -- not a placebo but a dose-matched active-drug comparator.
article.PrimaryCare: 0. Treatment was delivered as an inpatient psychiatric/medical protocol at a Veterans Administration Hospital by psychiatry service staff; no aspect interfaces with primary-care settings or providers.
article.Power: 0. No a priori or post hoc power calculation, sample-size justification, or discussion of statistical power appears anywhere in the Method, Results, or Discussion sections.
article.Retention (%): 62.5 = 45/72 x 100. Denominator is the randomized N (72; all 72 patients admitted were randomized/treated, so enrolled=randomized here -- 'Of the original 72 patients treated...'). Numerator is the 45 patients followed at the six-month timepoint tied to the primary Outcome and SampleSize_NFinal ('Only 45 patients were followed for six months, 27 dropping out'). The one-year retention (29/72=40.3%, from 17 LSD + 12 dextroamphetamine) was not used because the authors themselves judged the one-year sample 'too small and too selected to consider in detail.' Not within 2 points of 80, so no additional near-threshold flag applies.
article.MediatingYN: No candidate intermediate/mechanistic variable (e.g., mystical experience, therapeutic alliance) was ever measured, so coded 3 (no mediator to test) rather than 0.
article.InclusionExclusionCriteria: 1. Patients section states explicit inclusion criteria (men aged 21-50, VA-hospital-admission-eligible, acute alcoholic episode within 2 weeks, continuous area residency for 1 year, same job for >=6 months) and explicit disqualifying conditions (history of schizophrenic reaction or severe affective disorder, CNS disorder complicating alcoholism, serious medical illness such as severe hypertension, MI, or decompensated cirrhosis).
article.ValidatedScaleMeasYN: 0. The sole outcome instrument is the Drinking Behavior Scale (DBS), a measure the authors developed themselves for this line of research; its item selection and scoring were 'based on discussion among a number of colleagues' and later 'applied to known alcoholics for verification of the items and the scoring key,' but no reliability or validity statistics (e.g., internal consistency, test-retest, discriminant validity coefficients) are reported in this article, and the scale's full development/validation is deferred to a separate, explicitly 'unpublished' companion paper (Reference 1). Judgment call: coded 0 because no established, externally validated instrument or reported validation statistics appear in the article itself, as distinct from an ad hoc study-specific rating scale.
article.Funding/COI YN: 1. 'This work was supported in part by Public Health Service grant MH-05144 from the National Institute of Mental Health,' and the drug supplier is disclosed ('The drugs used in this study were furnished by Mr. Harry Althouse, Sandoz Pharmaceuticals, Inc.'). Funding-source disclosure alone satisfies this field; no separate COI statement is given.
article.BaseStatus: Coded '.'. The article explicitly states baseline severity spans the full range rather than clustering at one level: 'By any reckoning, all were problem drinkers, varying from the mildest to the most severe' (mean initial DBS 74, SD 29, range 20-174). No severity cut-points for the DBS are given anywhere in the article that would let a single bracket (Mild/Moderate/Severe) be assigned to the sample as a whole.
article.Age_Median: Bracket '30-50'. Table 1 (Background Variables): 'Age: median 45' for both the LSD and dextroamphetamine studied-case groups (range 31-51 / 33-51), squarely within the 30-50 bracket.
article.PercentFem: 0. Eligibility was restricted to 'Men between the ages of 21 and 50 years of age' -- an explicitly all-male sample.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: Coded '.'. No race or ethnicity data for the sample is reported anywhere in the article.
article.SocioeconomicStatusYN: 0. Table 1 reports employment status ('Unemployed') and educational attainment as general demographic descriptors, but no income figures, explicit low-income eligibility criterion, or public-insurance-enrollment information are reported anywhere. Judgment call: employment/education alone were not treated as an explicit SES description absent an income or insurance-status statement.
article.Country_USvsNonUS: US. 'The authors are with the Veterans Administration Hospital, Palo Alto, Calif. 94504.'
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: 0. Patients were VA-hospital admissions but subject to substantial exclusion criteria narrowing the sample away from a typical treatment-seeking alcoholic population: excluded were those with psychiatric comorbidity (schizophrenia, severe affective disorder), CNS disorder, or serious medical illness, and inclusion required demonstrated residential and occupational stability (continuous area residency for 1 year, same job for >=6 months) -- criteria selected specifically 'for assuring some degree of stability for future follow-up efforts' rather than to reflect the general clinical population of alcoholics presenting for care. Judgment call.
article.InterventionDescription: Summarized from the Treatment section: single oral dose of LSD-25 600mcg or dextroamphetamine 60mg, randomly assigned and blinded to the patient, administered in a dedicated furnished hospital room with music, under 8-hour constant attendance with two brief psychiatrist visits (30 minutes and 5 hours post-dose) for reassurance; inpatient VA hospital setting.
article.InterventionTherapy: 1. A structured preparatory discussion preceded drug administration, aimed at reframing the patient's problem drinking ('designed to minimize guilt... he had... been hooked by an addicting drug') and encouraging use of the drug state 'as a generally introspective experience,' plus two in-session psychiatrist visits explicitly intended 'to reinforce the introspective goals of therapy.' Judgment call, flagged because the authors themselves place 'psychotherapeutic' in scare quotes and state 'the patient was not assigned to any type of psychotherapy' and that 'no attempt at psychotherapy was made' during the visits -- the study's design intentionally minimized formal psychotherapy (per the abstract, 'little associated psychotherapeutic intervention') to isolate the drug's effect. Coded 1 because a preparatory/integration-oriented component beyond bare drug administration is nonetheless described, but this is explicitly a minimal, non-formal version of it.
article.HarmsAssessed: 1, consistent with SafetyReported='Y'. A dedicated paragraph in Results describes adverse events (agitation, chlorpromazine rescue, grand mal seizure, vomiting) and a further paragraph addresses the 'prolonged LSD reaction' question directly, including one patient's extended hospitalization for confusion. Two other patients' extended stays are explicitly attributed to arranging 'housing and other social considerations' rather than a medical/drug effect and were therefore not coded as adverse events in the ae_events array.
article.Followup in months: 12. The article reports outcome data at 2 months, 6 months, and 1 year (Table 4; 17 LSD and 12 dextroamphetamine patients followed to 1 year), making 12 months the longest reported follow-up horizon, even though the authors judge the 1-year subsample 'too small and too selected to consider in detail.' Measured from the single treatment day (no separate baseline-vs-end-of-treatment distinction applies, since the intervention was a single-day dose).
article.BehaviorChangeMeasured: 1. The Drinking Behavior Scale directly assesses drinking habits (use frequency/severity), social behavior, and occupational adjustment.
article.PhysicalChangeMeasured: 0. No biomarker, physiological measure, or vital-sign outcome is reported as a study outcome; vital-sign/medical details (chlorpromazine administration, seizure) are adverse-event/intervention-delivery information, not outcome measures.
article.MentalHealthChangeMeasured: 0. No depression, anxiety, PTSD, or general well-being scale is used as an outcome; the DBS assesses drinking habits, social behavior, and occupational adjustment specifically, not general mental-health symptomatology.
article.QualityOfLifeMeasured: 0. No dedicated quality-of-life instrument is used anywhere in the study.
article.Implementation Outcome: 0. No feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, reach, adoption, or sustainability outcome is discussed.
article.ReductionMeasured: 1. The DBS classification includes a 'social' category (DBS score of 10 or less, distinct from full abstinence) representing a partial reduction in drinking-related impairment as a distinct outcome category from 'abstinent.'
article.CessationMeasured: 1. The DBS classification includes an 'abstinent' category (a zero DBS score), directly measuring complete cessation.
article.RelapseMeasured: 1. Follow-up interviews explicitly tracked worsening/return-to-use ('worse' DBS category at each follow-up), and the Discussion explicitly names relapse: 'those observed at two months were somewhat better, with more tendency toward relapse at the six-month period.'
article.MortalityMeasured: 1. 'Five of the original 72 patients died within a year of entering the study... from some complications of alcohol (accidents, suicide, or decompensated cirrhosis).' Deaths are reported as a study-period finding; per the field rule this counts as 1 and generates a corresponding ae_events row (Hollister 1969_AE01).
article.LSD: 1. Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD-25), 600mcg, is one of the two randomized study interventions.
article.OtherPsychedelic: 0. Dextroamphetamine is the trial's other randomized arm, but per the task instructions it is not one of the nine keyed psychedelic substances and is not itself a psychedelic comparator (it is a stimulant), so it sets no substance flag. It is not routed to OtherPsychedelic because that column is reserved for psychedelic compounds outside the eight named ones, and dextroamphetamine is not a psychedelic at all.
article.MultiplePsychedelic: 0. Only one of the nine psychedelic substance flags (LSD) is set; dextroamphetamine, the comparator, is not a psychedelic and does not count toward this field.
article.SafetyReported: Y. Results contains a dedicated paragraph on drug-experience tolerability (agitation, chlorpromazine use, seizure, vomiting) and a further paragraph specifically addressing post-discharge safety ('prolonged LSD reaction', extended hospitalizations).
article.AnyAEReported: Y. Multiple distinct adverse events are described (agitation, seizure, vomiting, prolonged confusion/hospitalization, deaths).
article.NumDistinctAEs: 5 distinct AE types identified: agitation (incl. chlorpromazine-requiring subset), grand mal seizure, vomiting, prolonged confusion/extended hospitalization, and death. The two patients whose extended stay was attributed to housing/social arrangements (not a symptom or drug reaction) were not counted as a distinct AE type.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: Coded '.' rather than a summed total. The article does not provide a single unduplicated count of patients with >=1 AE: 'occasionally' (agitation) is not numbered, the seizure patient is very likely one of the two chlorpromazine-treated agitation patients (event described as occurring 'during one of these periods of agitation'), and death, vomiting, and hospitalization counts are separate and possibly overlapping subsets. Summing the printed per-event counts would double-count and fabricate a total the article never states.
article.AE_denominator: 72. All 72 randomized patients received their assigned single-dose treatment ('Of the original 72 patients treated...'); the safety narrative is not restricted to a smaller assessed subgroup.
article.ArmScope: pooled. The agitation/seizure/vomiting paragraph describes 'these patients' generically without disaggregating by LSD vs dextroamphetamine arm, and the treatment-day protocol (dosing, attendance, psychiatrist visits) was identical for both arms. The 'prolonged LSD reaction' paragraph is framed around addressing public concern specifically associated with LSD, but does not explicitly restrict the discharge/hospitalization figures to the LSD arm alone, and the deaths are likewise not attributed to a single arm. Judgment call, resolved toward 'pooled' because no AE value in the article is explicitly restricted to only the psychedelic-exposed subgroup.
article.WorstSeverity: Severe. Maximum severity across ae_events (death, AE01; seizure, AE03; hospitalization for confusion, AE05).
article.EligibleYN: Y. Criterion (a): a prospectively planned, randomized, blind single-dose trial with defined enrollment (72 patients), an assigned regimen (LSD-25 or dextroamphetamine), and prospective outcome assessment at 2, 6, and 12 months -- clearly a clinical trial. Criterion (b): the Drinking Behavior Scale directly measures drinking-related outcomes (abstinence, social/problem drinking categories), satisfying the substance-use-outcome requirement. Both criteria met.
article.SchemaRevisionNote: 2026-09-03 schema-revision splice: ConfoundYN/PVal removed, MediatingYN/ModeratingYN/HypothesisTestReportedYN added, sourced from a separate v3 extraction run (PromptVersion v1.3) rather than this file's own v1.2 run. Every other field in this file is unchanged from the original v1.2 extraction -- this file is now a hybrid of two runs for these 3 fields only. See clinical_adjudication.md '2026-09-03 -- Coding-scheme revision' for the full rationale.

ae_events.Hollister 1969_AE01: Attribution to the study drugs is not established by the authors -- they note 'such high mortality rates are common in long-term observations of alcoholics' and attribute 4 of 5 deaths to alcohol-related causes (accidents, suicide, decompensated cirrhosis) rather than to LSD or dextroamphetamine specifically, and the arm distribution of the 5 deaths is not reported. Included as an AE per the field rule that deaths reported during a trial's follow-up period generate an ae_events row and set MortalityMeasured=1, regardless of causal attribution, per the instruction that understating harm is the cardinal AE error. Severity=Severe reflects the rubric's death=Grade-5-equivalent classification (SeveritySource='rubric'), not an author-assigned CTCAE grade, since CTCAE did not exist in 1969 and the authors did not apply formal seriousness language to these deaths.
ae_events.Hollister 1969_AE02: Merged the 'occasionally, moderate agitation' description and the 'two patients... intramuscular chlorpromazine' detail into one 'agitation' AE type rather than splitting into two rows, since both describe the same underlying event (agitation during the dosing session) at varying severity/count granularity, and the article does not provide a total count separate from the two-patient chlorpromazine subset. Severity graded Moderate because a subset required active pharmacological intervention (chlorpromazine), per the rubric's 'requires active intervention... but meets no FDA seriousness criterion' band.
ae_events.Hollister 1969_AE03: Graded Severe per the rubric's explicit listing of seizure as a PAT-specific severe event, regardless of the article's own note that it occurred 'without injury.' SeveritySource='rubric' because the authors describe the event factually without assigning it a seriousness label themselves.
ae_events.Hollister 1969_AE05: The authors' own words are 'Moderate confusion was present in the third patient, requiring hospitalization for some further 48 hours' -- author-supplied severity language ('moderate') that would normally support SeveritySource='author' per the pre-1980 provision. However, the rubric's FDA-seriousness tiebreak ('Inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization... overrides the grade-based band upward, never downward') requires this event be coded Severe despite the authors' 'moderate' descriptor, because the confusion caused a prolongation of hospitalization. SeveritySource is therefore coded 'rubric' to reflect that the final band was set by applying the seriousness override rather than adopting the author's descriptor directly -- flagged here as a non-obvious severity call. The two other patients whose stay was extended for housing/social reasons were excluded from this event and from the ae_events array entirely, since the article attributes their delay explicitly to non-medical logistics, not to a drug effect or symptom.

config_proposal.note: The primary (six-month) outcome comparison is reported only as a non-significant ANOVA result without a printed F value ('Not significant, analysis of variance'), so no numeric statistic exists to convert. The two-month result (F=8.85, 1&50 df, p<.01) is a real, convertible F statistic, but it is not the study's designated primary outcome -- the authors explicitly identify six months as 'the least biasing and most feasible evaluation period' and report that the two-month difference had vanished by then -- so substituting it would misrepresent a superseded early/transient finding as the primary effect. Table 3's categorical (Abstinent/Social/Same/Worse) breakdown was also not used because the printed dextroamphetamine-arm counts (7+2+5+1=15) do not sum to the stated N=19, an internal inconsistency in the OCR'd table that precludes a defensible computed_or.
config_proposal.tier2_basis: Primary (six-month) comparison shows near-identical mean DBS change scores between arms (48 LSD vs 49 dextroamphetamine, NS by ANOVA); authors explicitly state the two-month LSD advantage 'vanished' by six months, and conclude 'LSD as a primary treatment... [has no] advantage over dextroamphetamine.'
